newsitem.title: USA: Gateway 2000 says to split stock, move to NYSE.
newsitem.headline: Gateway 2000 says to split stock, move to NYSE.

text.p: Gateway 2000 Inc., a direct marketer of personal computers, said its board authorised a two-for-one stock split and that its shares will begin trading on the New York Stock Exchange, fuelling a jump in its stock.
Gateway, based in North Sioux City, S.D., also said that its board authorised a stock repurchase programme to buy up to 10 million shares -- adjusted for the stock split -- of common stock.

Shares of the direct PC maker soared on the news, combined with some bullish comments by founder and Chief Executive Officer Ted Waitt about the outlook for the company at its annual meeting, analysts said. Gateway's shares soared $7.50 to $68.875 in heavy volume of over 6 million shares.

"The feedback I got was that Ted was relatively bullish about the big picture kind of stuff," said Mark Specker, a SoundView Financial analyst. "Plus, the split, the move to the NYSE, put all those elements together, that drove the shares right up."

Gateway said that Waitt discussed the company's plans in 1997 for an aggressive move into the corporate market, where it hopes to get more large corporate accounts. In 1996, about half of its sales were to business customers.
"That is one emphasis we have this year is in the corporate marketplace," said Rick Snyder, Gateway's president and chief operating officer, in a phone interview.
"We will be enhancing our product offerings and we are adding account people," Synder said.

"Gateway realises that the value is in the corporate space," said Daniel Ries, a Nomura Research analyst. More emphasis on big corporate sales means more predictable orders and not so much seasonal business, in the fourth quarter, when a big surge of orders comes during the back-to-school and holiday periods.

Rival Dell Computer Corp., the Austin, Texas based company that pioneered the direct model when founder and CEO Michael Dell started selling PCs out of his college dorm room, has an even bigger percentage of corporate customers.

Direct marketers of PCs build the systems as they are ordered by customers, to their specific configurations. They also ship the products to customers, eliminating corporate resellers, distributors and retailers, and have lower costs.

The stock of Gateway, which ships its PCs in boxes with a cow motif, has been incredibly volatile in recent months, as it was rumoured to be in takeover talks with Compaq Computer Corp. The world's leading PC maker is shifting its manufacturing to embrace a build-to-order model.

Time Magazine recently reported that the companies were close to a nearly $7 billion merger, but it fell apart at the last minute, as its pony-tailed CEO balked at having to report to Compaq CEO Eckhard Pfeiffer as his boss.

"Gateway 2000 is not for sale," Snyder said, but he declined to comment any further on whether Gateway talked with Compaq. Snyder said Gateway's move to the NYSE would help the stock become less volatile, trading in the "big leagues."

The move to the NYSE may enhance visibility of the company that likes to tout its home-spun culture. At the annual meeting, for example, Gateway said it showed stockholders the "Country Store" motif of its several retail showrooms, with PCs set up around tractor seats amid hay bales and farm silos.
"Maybe we will have a cow loose on Wall Street," Snyder said, when asked what the company's plans were to celebrate its move to the Big Board.
Gateway said that its stock split will be for shareholders of record on June 2 with distribution expected about June 16.
As of May 7, Gateway had about 77 million shares outstanding. After the split, the number will increase to about 154 million shares, it said.
